front.title: Signed Attestation Rows of the CIRIS Epistemic Grammar and Their Relationship to SCITT
front.workgroup: Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust

abstract.t: The CIRIS Epistemic Grammar (CEG) records claims between parties as signed rows. Each row is one or more COSE_Sign1 messages over a payload in deterministically encoded CBOR. Each message carries one composite ML-DSA-65 and Ed25519 signature. Every row has one of five types: a claim, a delegation, a replacement, a withdrawal, or a recantation. A node admits a row only after a fixed set of checks, and it refuses a failing row with a named reason.

This document specifies the signed statement, its encoding, the names by which rows refer to each other, the signature, and the admission checks, so that a second implementation can produce and verify the same bytes. It then describes how these statements relate to the roles of the SCITT architecture (RFC 9943), and where they differ. It defines no new SCITT mechanism and requests no IANA action.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: CEG is the row format of the CIRIS system, in which people, devices, communities and AI agents make claims about each other and act on them. It is defined normatively in the CIRIS Constitution . This document restates the parts of that definition that another implementation needs in order to interoperate at the byte level.
Three goals shape the format:

list.t: Any party holding a row can recompute its bytes and its name exactly. The payload and the protected header are in the deterministic encoding of CBOR, and a verifier refuses any other encoding of the same value ().

Rows exchanged between nodes have to resist forgery by an attacker with a quantum computer. Every statement carries one composite signature, ML-DSA-65 with Ed25519 , and neither half verifies alone ().
The set of row types is closed, so that every row is subject to the same admission rules. New kinds of claim are new families and dimensions, never new types.

section.t: SCITT defines an architecture for registering signed statements with a Transparency Service and returning receipts that prove registration. Each CEG statement is a COSE_Sign1 with an issuer and a subject in its protected header, so it has the shape of a SCITT Signed Statement. CEG fixes no Transparency Service, and its admission checks need none. A trust root's genesis bundle may name the services its heads are registered with, and a room may name them for its accountable streams (). A host that runs code a row admits first requires a SCITT receipt from a Transparency Service it trusts (). describes the relationship and what still differs.

section.name: Scope
section.t: In scope:

list.t: the signed statement of a row and its headers ();
the five row types ();
the deterministic encoding and the rules that close it ();
the row id, the statement id and the object id ();
the composite signature, keys and counted rows ();
the admission checks, written as a SCITT Registration Policy ().

section.t: Informative only:

list.t: the other signed objects and receipts ();
the safety properties the rows carry ();
the relationship to SCITT roles ();
the lifecycle of an agent's decision record ().

section.t: Out of scope: the transport between nodes, the storage schema, the meaning of individual claim families (the "dimension" namespace), and the governance rules that decide who may hold which role. defines each of these.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document uses the terms Issuer, Signed Statement, Transparency Service, Registration Policy, Receipt, Transparent Statement, and Relying Party as defined in . It also uses:

dd.t: One COSE_Sign1 under CBOR tag 18, made by one signer.
One signed attestation. A row is one statement, or several statements over one payload where the row is counted ().
The CBOR map a row's statements sign. It is carried as the COSE_Sign1 payload, as a byte string in the deterministic encoding.
The key that makes a statement. Its stable identity is the CWT iss claim. It plays the SCITT Issuer role.
What a row is about. The CWT sub claim names it. The payload member subject_key_ids lists any further subjects, including parties that have no key.
The one spelling of a key's identity: the COSE Key Thumbprint URI of for the key ().
The name of a row's claim family, carried in the protected header ().
A Producer emits rows. A Consumer verifies and reads rows. A Substrate stores and relays rows and applies the admission checks. One node is usually all three.

A fixed, case-sensitive ASCII string, so that two implementations agree on a refusal as well as on an acceptance. A reason is what a verifier gives for answering Invalid. A refusal token is what a Substrate gives for refusing a row. Every reason and token in this document is lower case, and is compared byte for byte. A reason may carry a detail after a colon, as in malformed:refs. lists them all, and says where one fault has both a reason and a token.

section.name: COSE_Sign1 and the Protected Header
section.t: A statement is a COSE_Sign1 under CBOR tag 18. Its payload is never detached. The protected header of a row's statement carries exactly seven members, and the signature covers all of them.

-70100, the composite algorithm of

"application/vnd.ciris.row+cbor", with no parameters
kid
The 32-byte thumbprint of the signing key ()
CWT claims
iss, sub, iat, and nbf and exp where the row has them, and the edition claim

"ceg-row/2"

One of the five row types, as a text string

section.t: The CWT claims are carried as defines. The edition claim has the label -70003 and the value 2. iat, nbf and exp are derived from payload members ().

A verifier MUST refuse a row whose cty carries parameters, or whose protected header lacks the type label or the family label. It MUST refuse a protected header with any other member, so that one statement has one statement id (). A signed object that is not a row carries neither label, and one that does is refused ().
sub names what the row is about: the attested key, or the object the row refers to. A statement's kind is its typ .

section.name: The Family Id
section.t: The family label carries a family id, never a leaf. A family id is the family's registry prefix in , with each {name} segment written as a full stop followed by the name, and each * written as a lone full stop. Examples are key:record and provenance:build_manifest:.target.

A literal segment never begins with a full stop, so no two prefixes share a family id. A row that scores a dimension carries it whole, leaf and version, in the payload member dimension. A verifier MUST refuse a dimension that does not resolve to the family id the header carries.

A withdraws or a recants row carries the family id of its target and no dimension, and its sub is its target's. One that states a dimension is Invalid, malformed:dimension. A supersedes row is a row of its own family and carries its own dimension (CC 2.6.1.1).

section.name: Identity References
section.t: iss is the signer's stable identity reference: the COSE Key Thumbprint URI of for the signer's genesis key. It is urn:ietf:params:oauth:ckt:sha-256: followed by the unpadded base64url of the 32-byte thumbprint. That is 43 characters, the last with zero trailing bits.

Because iss names the genesis key, the issuer stays the same when the signing key rotates; kid names the key that signs. author, a key named by sub or by an element of subject_key_ids, and every role party use this one spelling. A verifier MUST refuse any other.

iss is a claim. The signature shows which key signed, and kid names that key. That the key is a key of the identity iss names is a separate check of verification (). A statement that fails it is Invalid, whatever its signature.

In a private room a person signs with a room key made for that room. On a row a room key signs, iss is the voice: the identity reference of the voice's first room key. It is never the person's (CC 2.6.1.11).

section.name: The Unprotected Header and External AAD
section.t: external_aad is the empty byte string, and no party puts a domain prefix there. The unprotected header is outside the signature, and no admission check reads it. A holder may add a receipt there, or present a disclosure there (, ). A host reads a receipt there before it runs code a row admits; the receipt grants nothing, and a malformed one is ignored ().
There is no copy of the headers inside the payload and no signature beside the statement. The protected header and the payload are the row. A further voice is a further statement ().

section.name: The Payload
section.t: The payload is a CBOR map whose members the row's family names. Every row carries asserted_at. Other members that fixes for every family include:

dd.t: The iss of the one who authors the row. It is present when the family is authored and absent when the family is counted ().
Every row this row names ().
The full scored dimension, leaf and version. It resolves to the header's family id.
The blobs the row cites, by content hash, as a sequence.
Integers at a fixed scale ().
Instants ().
Sixteen random bytes. A row whose content is low-entropy, such as a ballot or a census cell, carries one, so that its row id confirms no guess.
A map whose member note holds at most 2048 bytes of free text. No free text stands outside body.note.
A code from a closed registry.

section.t: subject_key_ids, cohort_scope, scope and the claim's other members are payload members of the same names. gives the full schema. A Consumer MUST preserve members it does not recognise when it relays a row ().

section.name: The Five Row Types
section.t: The row type label (-70001) takes exactly one of five values, compared byte for byte. A statement that carries any other value does not meet the header's schema. A verifier answers Invalid at step 2 of , with the reason malformed:row-type. A Substrate MUST refuse such a row, both where it emits the row and where it receives it, and it reports the refusal with the token attestation_type_unregistered (CC 2.4). The reason and the token name one fault ().

dd.t: A claim about the subject on the named dimension. Every positive or negative claim about a party is a scores row.

The signer authorises the subject to sign on its behalf within scope, a set of strings. For the scopes that lists as requiring a term, among them licensing, moderation and takedown, the delegation's end is REQUIRED. It MUST be no more than 365 days after its start. A Substrate refuses a row that breaks this with delegation_term_required.
The signer replaces one of its own earlier rows, named by row id in refs.
The signer retracts an earlier row, named by row id in refs, without saying the row was false. says who may withdraw a row.
The signer says one of its own earlier rows was false when it was made. Only the original signer can recant a row.

section.t: A withdrawal and a recantation are different statements. A withdrawal says "I no longer assert this"; a recantation says "this was wrong". The subject of a row has authority over the first but not the second ().

None of the three removes its target: the target stays held and verifiable, and each names it in refs.target (). A verifier reports a row's state as one of four: admitted, superseded, withdrawn or recanted (CC 2.7.5). The state is derived, not final, since a later row on the same target, concurrent with the first, can change it. Consumers may weigh a withdrawn and a recanted row differently; they MUST NOT report either as admitted.
A new kind of record is expressed as a new family or dimension on one of the five types, never as a sixth type.

section.name: Deterministic Encoding
section.t: The payload is encoded in CBOR's deterministic encoding, as the Common Deterministic Encoding fixes it over . A verifier MUST refuse a payload whose bytes differ from the deterministic re-encoding of the value they decode to. That covers a non-shortest integer, an indefinite length, an unsorted map key and a duplicate key.

The protected header is in the deterministic encoding too. A second encoding of one value would otherwise be a second row. A verifier verifies the bytes it received, never a re-encoding of members it decoded.

section.name: The Omit Rule
section.t: The bytes are the members the Producer signs. An optional member the Producer omits MUST NOT be written into the payload by any party. An optional member the Producer emits, even at its default value, MUST be kept by every party. Defaults documented in are applied when a row is read, never when it is encoded.

An optional member is unset by being absent, never by null. A payload with null for an optional member is Invalid, malformed: and the member (). A Substrate MUST refuse it, with the token federation_malformed_row and the reason envelope_member_null. No value a family names, at any depth, is a float, a null, an undefined value, a tag or a simple value. The exceptions are the redaction marks of and the decimal fraction of .

A Substrate, relay or Consumer that stores or forwards a statement MUST forward the octets it received. It never strips an emitted default and never writes in an omitted one. Unknown members are kept the same way.

section.name: Sets, Sequences and Tuples
section.t: An array whose positions the schema names is a tuple, and its order is its definition. An array of one element type is a set or a sequence, as its definition states. Where no definition says, it is a set.

list.t: A set is sorted by the bytewise order of its elements' deterministic encodings and holds no duplicate. A verifier answers Invalid for any other, set_order: and the member, and a Substrate refuses it with the token federation_set_semantics_unsorted, naming the member (). Neither ever re-sorts the set, because that would change the signed bytes.
A sequence keeps its authored order. The sequences are evidence_refs, the redacted-key arrays of , and the others lists.

section.t: Every array inside refs is a set ().

section.name: Bytes and Text
section.t: A byte member is a CBOR byte string. Hexadecimal and base64 do not stand in the payload for bytes.

subject_key_ids is the one member with two forms. An element naming a registered key carries that key's identity reference (). An element naming a party with no key is the tagged text canonical:<hashalg>:<hex>. The tag is part of the signed string, and the hex is lowercase.

section.name: Numbers
section.t: No member of the payload is a float. A score, a confidence and a weight are integers at the fixed scale of 10^6: the value times 10^6. A score lies in [-10^6, 10^6], a confidence in [0, 10^6] and a weight in [0, 10^6], unless the family states a wider range.

A number in a free-form body that is not an integer is a decimal fraction: CBOR tag 4 over [exponent, mantissa], with a negative exponent and a mantissa in CBOR's integer range that is not divisible by 10. An integral number is a plain integer. A number outside CBOR's integer range, alone or as a mantissa, is refused body_number_unrepresentable. A decimal fraction that is not normalised is a second encoding of one value, and is refused as any other is, not_deterministic:payload (CC 2.6.1.2).

A fold sums in signed 64-bit integers, and its arithmetic is checked: a fold that would overflow is refused, and never wraps. A derived value is computed in integers and checked by exact equality. It is rounded half away from zero unless its own rule states otherwise.

section.name: Instants
section.t: asserted_at, valid_from, valid_until, expires_at and every other instant in a payload are unsigned integers of POSIX milliseconds, never floats. The header's iat, nbf and exp are the standard CWT claims in seconds. Each is the floor of its payload member divided by 1000. A verifier MUST refuse a statement whose header claim disagrees with its payload member.
Where an instant stands in signed text rather than in a payload, fixes a separate text form. No statement of this document carries one.

section.name: Size
section.t: A payload's deterministic encoding MUST NOT exceed 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes). The bound is on the bytes the signature covers. A Producer MUST NOT emit a larger payload. A Substrate MUST refuse one at every write path, with envelope_too_large ().

Every write path MUST also enforce a finite ceiling on the octets it buffers from an untrusted source. It refuses at that ceiling in the same way, without completing the decode. The ceiling is local, MUST NOT be below 1 MiB, and SHOULD be published.
Larger content travels outside the row and is named in evidence_refs by its hash.

section.name: Erasable Members
section.t: A family may mint some members blind, using the selective disclosure of . A blinded member is absent from its map. Its disclosure is the salted claim [salt, value, key], with a salt of sixteen random bytes. Its digest stands in that map's redacted_claim_keys array, keyed by the simple value 59, in mint order.

A blinded array element is tag 60 over its disclosure's digest, and its disclosure is [salt, value]. A digest is SHA-256 over the disclosure's bytes. A disclosure travels beside its statement, in the unprotected header's sd_claims (label 17), only to one who may see it.
Erasure drops a disclosure and alters no signed byte. Which members are blind is fixed by the family in . No fold, verdict or admission reads a member that can be blinded.

section.name: The Row Id
section.t: A row is named by one digest, its row id. It is SHA-256 over the deterministic encoding of this array:

type and family are the text strings of labels -70001 and -70002. sub is the CWT subject. author is the payload's author, or null. payload enters as the byte string signed, never as the decoded map. A digest is written as the array [-16, digest], where -16 names SHA-256.

Signatures, kid, alg, receipts and disclosures are outside the row id. So every voice of a counted row has the same row id. The row id does not change when a voice, a receipt or a disclosure is added. The row id commits to iat, nbf and exp, because they are derived from payload members. It does not read cty.

section.name: The Statement Id
section.t: A statement's own id is SHA-256 over the deterministic encoding of ["CEG-statement-id/2", protected, payload], written the same way. protected and payload are the byte strings of the statement. It names one voice; the row id names the row.

This is the CEG statement id, a name of this profile: defines no statement identifier. It covers the protected header and the payload. It leaves out the signature and the unprotected header, so a receipt or a disclosure added later does not change it. The external_aad of a CEG statement is the empty byte string (), so a CEG statement id and a reference to the COSE Sig_structure of the same statement select the same statements, though the two encoded inputs differ.

A match on a statement id, a row id or an object id says that two parties name the same bytes. It says nothing of who signed them. That a statement's key is a key of its iss, and that its signature verifies, are steps of verification ().

section.name: What a Row Names
section.t: Every row a row names stands in one payload member, refs, by reference. A reference is the array [2, digest]: the edition and the row id. refs is a map with these members:

texttable.title: Members of refs
texttable.c: head
The head the row is at: the head a count is over (), the head an act is exercised at, or the head an end acts from ()
further_heads
Further tips beside head
prev
The predecessor in a signer's own series; on a content row, a content row its author signed in the same room
further_prev
Further content rows of the same author in the same room, beside prev
answers
The row this row answers: the proposal voted on or accepted, the window opened, the row replied to
target

The row a supersedes, withdraws or recants row names; on a rotation record, the old key's record (); the act a cut ends or the member a removal removes; and, on a halt's confirmation or resumption, that halt ()
trusted_through
On a key revocation, the last rows of the key held good; on a row that ends a member's seat and on a keeps row, the member's newest content rows held good. At most 64
also
A map from a role to a set of references. The roles are ack, cites, under, stands_on and voice

section.t: A holder reads the set of named rows from refs alone, without knowing the family. target is not confined to the three row types that replace or retract: a rotation record is a key record that names its predecessor there.
The roles of also are a closed registry of five (CC 2.6.1.3):

list.t: ack names a row acknowledged, as a receipt of acts does ().
cites names a row the row cites.
under names the one edge a deputy's edge hangs from. It is a set of exactly one.
stands_on names the one acceptance that a row signed under a root grant stands on. It is a set of exactly one ().
voice names the head of the key roster of the voice a room key signs for. It is a set of exactly one ().

section.t: A role is a key of the also map and is not a member of refs. Any other role is Invalid, unexpected:also.

A row waits for the rows it names, with two exceptions that are named for the fold alone: prev and further_prev on a content row, and trusted_through on a row that ends a seat or a keeps row (CC 2.7.3).

Every array inside refs is a set, and a set out of order is refused. An empty refs is refused: absence is its one encoding. An empty set inside refs, and an empty also, are refused in the same way. No row names an object of the earlier form of .

section.name: The Author
section.t: A family is either authored or counted, as states for each family. An authored family's payload carries author, the iss of the one who authors the row. The row id reads it from the payload. A counted family's author is null.
Where a family is authored by its subject, the row is authored by the attested key: author MUST be the CWT sub, and a statement whose iss is another key is Invalid.

A statement whose iss is not the payload's author is accepted only in a role its family names, such as a delegate or a bound node. Its iss MUST then be the party that role names in the payload. Where that party is the attested key, as a delegate is, it MUST be the CWT sub. On an authored row that its family counts, a voice of that count is accepted too. Any other iss is Invalid, iss_not_in_role (, CC 2.6.1.3).

section.name: The Composite Signature
section.t: A statement's signature is the composite ML-DSA-65 with Ed25519 of , over , at the revisions cited. It is computed over the Sig_structure of , with an empty external_aad. That Sig_structure is the message M.
Both halves sign one message representative:

The zero byte is the empty application context. ML-DSA-65 signs M' with the label bytes as its FIPS 204 context string, never the empty one. Ed25519 signs M' as it is. The representative binds both halves, so neither half verifies alone.

The encoding is the ML-DSA-65 signature (3309 bytes) followed by the Ed25519 signature (64 bytes), 3373 bytes in all. The algorithm identifier is -70100, a private-use value. A key's thumbprint covers the identifier, so kid and iss carry it, and a new identifier would rename every identity. A lineage therefore keeps -70100 for its keys. A move to an assigned identifier is a planned migration, by a later genesis bundle that seats the renamed keys (CC 2.6.1.7). ML-DSA-65 alone is COSE algorithm -49 ; CEG does not use it alone.

section.name: Keys
section.t: A key is one composite COSE key of key type AKP (kty 7). Its pub (label -1) is the ML-DSA-65 public key followed by the Ed25519 public key, 1984 bytes. Its kid is its 32-byte SHA-256 thumbprint , fixed for the key's life. The thumbprint is over the deterministic encoding of the key with exactly its three members, {1: 7, 3: -70100, -1: pub}. A key's displayed identity is that thumbprint.

section.name: Key Records
section.t: A key record is a row of the family key:record. Its sub is the identity reference of the key it records. Its payload carries key, identity_type, asserted_at and, where its end rule requires, valid_until.

identity_type is a set of roles. A set that mixes a person's role (user or accord_holder) with a machine's (node or agent) is refused, key_record_mixed_roles. A record whose set contains a person's role carries no valid_until. One whose set contains node or agent carries one, unless it is a room key of a private room. A pseudonym's record MAY carry one, and a role outside both groups takes no end rule of its own. Where valid_until is present it is later than asserted_at, and no more than key_record_max_secs after it, a constant of . A record whose valid_until is not later than its asserted_at is Invalid at step 4 of , valid_until_not_after_asserted_at. One that otherwise breaks the rule is refused key_record_out_of_window (CC 2.4.1.1). The check of a key record's payload alone has no step 4, and answers key_record_out_of_window for either fault.

Each key's own holder signs its record. A record makes its key live only where a statement over it by that key itself is held. A record that only other keys have signed makes the key live nowhere, and no third party ends a key or revives one (CC 2.4.1.1).
A record covers an instant that is at or after its asserted_at and, where it states valid_until, before it. The end is not covered: a record whose valid_until is T does not cover T.

A key is live at an instant when one of its records covers that instant and its own revocation has not taken effect by then. Only the key's own revocation ends its liveness. The key's owner and the roster that seats it may also revoke it. That ends the owner's binding or the seat, not the key's liveness. A revocation signed by any other key concludes nothing, key_revocation_no_standing.
A key renews by signing a further record that supersedes its own earlier record. Renewals that do not name each other all count, and the key lives to the greatest end they state.

section.name: Rotation
section.t: iss names the signer's genesis key and stays the same when the signing key changes. A rotation is what links the next key to that iss. A rotation record has one shape (CC 3.1.3). It is the key record of the new key, and:

list.t: Its payload names the old key's record in refs.target, by row id ().
Its iss is the iss of the old key's record, in every statement over it.
It carries two statements over the one payload. One is the new key's own, which shows possession of the new key. The other is the old key's.

The record it names is a valid record of the old key under that iss, and it covers the rotation record's asserted_at. That is the instant of the old key's statement, which is thereby made inside the old key's record.

section.t: A record of any other shape links no key to an iss. One that names no predecessor never does. One that lacks either statement does not until that statement is held ().

A rotation hands on what the old key may hand on, and never extends the old key. A renewal on the way, a supersedes by a key of its own record, leaves the chain where it was. A link stands where its predecessor's statement stands: made inside the predecessor's record, and before the revoked_after of a revocation by that key itself. So a link made while its predecessor was live stands after that key has ended, and no other voice's revocation cuts a chain.

Two rotations of one key, neither naming the other, are contested. They hand on nothing until a rotation names both. A statement that a contested successor signs under the old iss is Invalid, kid_not_of_iss. A rotation is such a rival only where it meets item 4: one that names a record of the old key that does not cover its own instant blocks nothing (CC 2.4.1.1).

section.name: The Key of an Issuer
section.t: A statement's key MUST be a key of its iss. A signature that verifies shows only that the holder of kid's key signed. It does not show that the key belongs to the identity iss claims, and without this check a statement signed by one party could name another as its issuer. The key that kid resolves to is a key of iss in one of four ways:

list.t: kid is the thumbprint inside iss. The key is the genesis key, or a room key signing as itself.
The verifier holds a key record of that key whose own iss is the statement's iss, and that record reaches the genesis key's record through rotation records, each of the shape of .
The genesis bundle in force seats that key for that iss, as a recovery or a rotation by bundle does (). The seat ends at the first later bundle in force that does not seat the key.

A live occurrence of iss binds that key: an identity:occurrence row of iss that the verifier holds, whose occurrence_key_id is the key. The row is admitted, not evicted, and covers the statement's instant. It carries the bound key's own statement over the same payload, as proof of possession.

section.t: A node or agent key is never a key of an identity whose genesis record is a person's.
Where none of the four holds, the answer is Waiting or Invalid, and what the verifier holds decides which.

dd.t: The answer is Waiting where a row that one of the ways needs is known to the verifier and not held. Waiting names that row. It is one of these: the record that a held rotation record names; a statement that a held rotation record lacks, the new key's own or the old key's; a statement that a held occurrence lacks, the bound key's own or one of iss; an occurrence that covers the statement's instant, where the one held has ended; a row that the admission of an occurrence needs; and the bundle in force, where the verifier knows of it and does not hold it. A row gains statements without changing its row id, so a record that lacks a statement waits for it and is not refused (CC 3.1.3, CC 2.6.1.9).

Otherwise the statement is Invalid, kid_not_of_iss. Nothing that the verifier could name is missing: each held record of the key is of another identity, or the record names no predecessor, or the chain does not reach the genesis key, or the rotation is contested, or the occurrence that binds the key is of another identity or evicted. Where a link fails only by its predecessor's own revoked_after, the reason carries the detail rotation_after_revocation.

A verifier that holds bare keys and no rows can show only the first way. It holds no row that names another, so it can name nothing as missing. For a statement whose kid is not the thumbprint inside iss, its answer is Invalid, kid_not_of_iss.

section.t: kid_not_of_iss is an answer over the rows held. states that a contested rotation is kid_not_of_iss until a rotation names both, so a later row can change it. A bad signature is different: that answer is final ().
The statements of a genesis bundle and of the accord's rows bind their key to the holder by the bundle in force instead (CC 2.6.1.11, CC 4.2.1.1).

section.name: Counted Rows
section.t: A counted row is several statements over one payload, one for each voice, found by the row id. The head the row is counted over stands in refs.head, inside what every voice signs. Further tips stand in refs.further_heads, a set. A fold counts the statements by person, as it counts votes.

Each statement is a SCITT Signed Statement with one signer. Adding a voice changes neither the payload nor the row id. A delegation of a scoped kind seats only with a second statement over the same payload, signed by the delegate, the row's sub.
Two statements over different payloads are two rows, whatever else they share.

section.name: Verification Has Three Answers
section.t: Verifying a statement gives one of three answers: Valid, Invalid with a reason, or Waiting on what it names as missing. What is missing is a key at step 6 below, and a row or a statement of a row at step 8.

list.t: A bad signature under a held key is Invalid, and that answer is final. A structural fault is Invalid whatever keys are held.
A statement whose key record is Waiting is Waiting, naming the deepest missing key. A statement whose key record is Invalid is Invalid, key_not_valid.
A key is one composite key. A statement whose signer's key record is not held is Waiting on it, and a key never verifies on one half.
Waiting never becomes Valid by default and is never counted. A waiting statement is held inert until what it names is held.

section.t: A verifier proceeds in this order:

list.t: Decode strictly: tag 18, and the protected header and the payload in the deterministic encoding.
Check the header: typ on the closed list; alg -70100; edition 2; cty the constant; a row's type and family labels present, the type one of the five and the family registered; an object's absent.
Check the payload against the schema: no float or null, the sets, the ranges, passed and total, dimension resolving to the header's family, and the family's own payload rule.
Check iat, nbf and exp against the payload, and that a valid_until is later than asserted_at.
Run the family's static checks, the key record's end among them.

Read kid and resolve the key record: a record of that key that the key itself signed and that covers the statement's asserted_at. Answer Waiting where the key is not held, where its own statement over a held record is not held, or where no held record covers the instant.
Verify the composite signature over the bytes received.
Check that kid's key is a key of iss (). Answer Waiting on a chain link, a statement, the bundle in force or an occurrence that is not held; otherwise Invalid, kid_not_of_iss.
Check iss against author, or against the party of a role the family names ().
On Valid, apply the defaults of to absent members, at interpretation time only, and then the Consumer's own policy.
Store or forward the statement as received.

section.t: A failure at steps 1 to 5 or 7 to 9 is Invalid. Steps 6 and 8 alone answer Waiting. The reason is that of the first step that fails.

Step 6 is where a key's liveness at the statement's instant is read. A statement whose asserted_at no held record of its key covers is not Invalid. It waits for a record that covers the instant, as a statement signed by a key not yet held waits for the key (CC 2.4.1.1). A renewal signed later can supply that record. A verifier that holds bare keys reads no record, so it reads no instant at this step.
A Waiting answer says what is missing. The vectors of write it as waiting:, the kind of thing missing and, in the row statement files, what identifies it.

section.t: <kid> is the thumbprint of the key that is missing, of the key whose statement is missing, or of the key that lacks a covering record. <row id> is the row id of the record named. Each is 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits. <instant> is the statement's asserted_at, in decimal. voice is the vectors' word for one signer's statement over a row. The later key-of-issuer file of writes each answer by its kind alone: waiting:kid, waiting:voice, waiting:record, waiting:bundle, and waiting:covering for a covering record.

One further Waiting answer lies outside the eleven steps. It arises when a row is read under its family. A withdraws or a recants row takes the family of its target (). Where that family's authorship turns on the target's dimension and the target is not held, the reading waits on the target, as a row waits for the rows it names (). The vectors write it waiting:row:<row id>.

section.name: Other Signed Objects and Receipts
section.t: This section is informative. is normative for each object.

section.name: Objects That Are Not Rows
section.t: Every other signed object is a COSE_Sign1 whose typ names its kind, from one closed list: ceg-genesis-bundle/2, ceg-revocation-snapshot/2 and ceg-boot-manifest/2. A verifier MUST refuse any other typ. The protected header carries exactly alg, kid, the CWT claims and typ, with no cty. Its CWT claims are iss, the edition claim, and iat where the object states an instant.

Such an object is named by its object id: SHA-256 over the deterministic encoding of ["CEG-object/2", typ, author, payload]. author is the payload's author, or null where it has none. Like a row id, it is the same for every voice of a counted object.

section.name: The Genesis Bundle
section.t: A trust root is the lineage of a genesis bundle, named by the bundle's family_key_id, and that is the only kind of root (CC 3.2). A key that signs a charter about itself is no root.

The bundle's payload is a closed map. holders is the root's roster and serve_nodes its seats, each a set of identity references. charter carries the root's parameters, which no row carries: the recovery commitment of each holder, the scope, attach_window_secs, halt_fuse_secs and, where the root names Transparency Services, transparency_services, receipt_quorum and receipt_cadence_secs (). Every row the bundle seats stands in refs.also under cites, by row id: the key record of each holder, seat and named service, and the transport binding of each seat. holders, serve_nodes and transparency_services are disjoint. A seat stands by the bundle that names it, and the end of the seat's key record does not unseat it (CC 2.6.1.11).
The bundle is counted: one statement for each holder, over one payload. Each statement carries iat, equal to the payload's asserted_at divided by 1000 and rounded down.

The first bundle counts when every holder it lists has a valid statement over it. A later bundle names its predecessor as refs.prev. It counts when a strict majority of the predecessor's holders have valid statements over it. Each holder it adds signs it too.

A roster change is such a later bundle, with no proposal, window or separate vote. A holder's recovery is also a later bundle, with one statement under the holder's recovery key. That statement counts only where the predecessor's recovery commitment for the holder matches. Two later bundles that count on one predecessor are a fork, and a reader reports it.

A reader's anchor is what it was built or configured to trust: the object id of one first bundle, or the set of its holders' thumbprints. Under a thumbprint anchor, a first bundle verifies only where its holders equal the anchored set and every one of them signed it. Two first bundles that both do so are a fork of the genesis, and the reader roots on neither. A reader with no root runs no agent and serves no directory or seat of that root until its owner re-anchors it by an object id (CC 2.6.1.11).

Each holder's key carries an attestation chain for its classical half. Where the chain's leaf names its device, the holders a bundle seats name distinct devices; a bundle that seats two holders on one device is refused holder_device_shared. Two holders' chains may share an intermediate or an attestation key, and the leaf's device decides (CC 4.2.3).

A malformed bundle is Invalid, genesis_bundle_malformed, with a detail. Two of the details concern the transparency members. A charter that carries only some of the three is transparency_members_partial. A receipt_quorum that is not floor(n/2) + 1 of the n services named is receipt_quorum_mismatch (CC 2.6.1.11).

section.name: The Node Code
section.t: A key's displayed identity is its thumbprint (). The code a person hands over is CIRIS-V4- followed by the unpadded base32 of a payload and its CRC. The payload is a version byte of 4, a kind, and the 32-byte thumbprint of the identity's key. A user code may also name up to four of its owner's nodes, and a node code names one node. For each node the code gives the node's transport identity and an ordered list of up to eight hints for reaching it.

A hint is a type, a length and a body. The eight assigned types are 1 tcp, 2 udp, 3 auto, 4 rnode, 5 http, 6 i2p, 7 kiss and 8 ble. A decoder carries a hint of any other type as unknown, and a dialler skips it. A hint of a known type whose body is malformed is refused. A hint is unsigned and is only a place to dial. A minter writes hints from the node's configured, stable reachability, and never an observed address mapping.

A code is unsigned and confers no authority. First contact is a route request made before the link is sealed, anchored on the node thumbprint the code carries: the dialler keeps the key record it receives only where that record's thumbprint equals the code's. A decoder of this form refuses the codes of the earlier forms by their prefix (CC 2.6.8).

The same hints stand in a signed row as dial_hints on a node's transport binding: a sequence of one to eight, each a type and a body, byte for byte those of the code. The binding of a serve seat in a genesis bundle carries at least one tcp hint, and a bundle whose seat lacks one is refused with the detail seat_dial_hints_missing (CC 2.6.1.11).

section.name: Receipts
section.t: A receipt is a COSE Receipt over the SHA-256 tree of . Its hashing is that of . A Transparency Service keeps its own append-only log, registers a Signed Statement in it as one leaf, and issues a Receipt for that leaf under its own key. The Receipt states the service's identity, the subject of the registered statement and the service's own instant of issue. No service signs over another party's root. A stream's receipts cover batches, never single chunks (CC 2.6.1.11, CC 5.3.1).
A holder may add a receipt to a statement's unprotected header. The receipt is outside the signature and outside the row id.

A host does not run code a row admits until it holds a receipt for a statement of that row from a Transparency Service the host trusts. The receipt is the SCITT receipt itself: a COSE Receipt in the unprotected header's receipts parameter (label 394), as carries it. The service registers the statement's deterministic COSE_Sign1 encoding with an empty unprotected header, its leaf hash SHA-256(0x00 || leaf) as hashes a leaf. The host's own acceptance edge carries the service's key, a COSE_Key with its algorithm or an identity reference, and a receipt under another algorithm does not verify. The unprotected header is unsigned, so a malformed receipt is ignored and never makes the statement invalid. A missing or unverifiable receipt is not held: the code waits, with the answer admission_receipt_missing.

A host trusts a Transparency Service by its owner's own acceptance edge of the class transparency: one hop, read at the host's self scope, whatever the edge's tier. The edge carries the service's key as service_key, either a COSE_Key with its algorithm or an identity reference whose key is that identity's key record. Anyone may run a Transparency Service under their own key, and no list of services ships with anything. A receipt adds no authority: it witnesses that the statement was registered, which closes a release seen only by those it was sent to (CC 2.7.11, CC 4.4.3.34).

section.name: Registered Heads
section.t: A signer of a head could show one history to one party and another to a second. Registration with Transparency Services exposes that: each service keeps its own log, and two heads at one position that are both registered leave two Receipts under one service's key.

dd.t: A root's charter may name transparency_services, a set of at least two identity references, each to a composite key. receipt_quorum is exactly floor(n/2) + 1 of the n services named. receipt_cadence_secs is how often a named service issues a Receipt again for an unchanged head. The three members are present together or not at all. A lineage's head is the bundle in force, and a holder's statement over the bundle is the Signed Statement a service registers. A service registers one head for each lineage and position, and refuses a second.

A head is receipted when Receipts for it are held from receipt_quorum distinct independent services. The services are those the charter of the head's predecessor names, and for a first bundle its own charter. A service is independent of a lineage when it is none of the lineage's holders or seats and none of them owns it. Two heads of one lineage at one position that each hold a receipt quorum are equivocation: at least one service registered both, and its two Receipts name it.

A Consumer attaches to a root only on a receipted head whose newest counted Receipt was issued within the charter's attach_window_secs before the acceptance edge's own signed instant. A root already attached stays valid until revoked, whatever the age of its Receipts.

A charter that carries none of the three members names no services. Its head is current when the holders have counted it and it descends from a head the reader holds out of band. A holder majority that shows two heads to two nodes is then not detectable on the wire until a row crosses between them. Naming a service confers no standing on it and places no duty on anyone (CC 3.2, CC 5.3.1).

A stream is its own log, and its chunks are the leaves. A stream's head is a signed row of the family stream:head, authored by the stream's producer. It carries the stream's epoch, its tree size and its root. A stream's id is av- or file- followed by 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits. An inline blob's one-leaf log is named by 64 hexadecimal digits alone, and an inline file publishes no head.

A head that carries room is accountable, and one without it is best-effort. A room may name transparency_services and receipt_quorum in its record, for its accountable streams only, with the quorum again floor(n/2) + 1. An accountable head counts as published when receipt_quorum distinct services of the room have registered it. A service the producer or the producer's owner runs does not count. A service registers one head for each stream and tree size, and each later head is offered with a consistency proof from the head it last registered. A room keeps no attach window, cadence or quorum for its roster (CC 5.3.3.8).

section.t: A node's own audit log of its rows is no Transparency Service: it issues no Receipt and takes none.

section.name: Admission as a Registration Policy
section.t: lets each Transparency Service define a Registration Policy: the checks a Signed Statement must pass before it is registered. The CEG admission checks are such a policy. A Substrate MUST apply them to every row before storing or relaying it. It MUST NOT truncate, repair or re-encode a row in order to admit it.
The checks run in the order of . Each has one reason. A verifier reports invalid: followed by the reason, and the vectors of carry the same strings.

section.name: How a Reason Is Written
section.t: A name in angle brackets stands for the part, member, map or claim at fault.

<part> is statement, protected or payload: the encoded item that is not in the deterministic encoding. A float and a decimal fraction that is not normalised are second encodings of the payload, not_deterministic:payload.
<claim> is iat, nbf or exp.

<map> is the closed map that holds a key it does not admit: protected, unprotected, refs or also. A protected header that lacks a member it requires is unexpected:protected as well, since the header holds exactly its members.
<member> follows one rule. It is the innermost member of the row that the schema of names and whose value holds the fault. The row is the protected header and the payload ().

A member of the protected header or of the CWT claims has an integer label, and is named alg, cty, kid, typ, row-type (label -70001), family-id (label -70002), iss, sub, iat, nbf, exp or edition (label -70003).
A fault in an element of an array is reported under the member that holds the array.
A role of also is a key of a registry and not a member (). A fault in a role's set is reported as also.
A required member that is absent from the payload is reported under its own name, as in malformed:asserted_at.

section.t: Where no member that the schema names holds the fault, the name is that of the rule of that the value fails. There are two such places. A family's own member is typed by the schema as ceg-value and is not named by it, so a fault in its value, at any depth, is malformed:ceg-value. A disclosure travels beside the row and is no member of it, so a fault in one is malformed:sd-disclosure. The key of a family's own member never stands in a reason, and the reasons stay a closed set.
A statement with more than one fault is Invalid at the first step that fails. This document fixes no order among the faults of one step.

Three prefixes say at which level an answer was given. A statement read alone answers valid, invalid: and a reason, or waiting: and what is missing. A statement read under its family answers the checks of step 9 as family_invalid: and the reason, and where a role admits its signer it answers valid:role: and the role's name. The check of a key record's payload alone answers ok or the bare reason. The files of write them so, and the later key-of-issuer file writes family: for family_invalid:. Several statements read as one row, where their payloads differ, answer several_rows ().

section.name: Who May Withdraw a Row
section.t: A withdraws row against a target row T is admitted when its signer meets one of these rules:

dd.t: If T is a counted row, rules 1 to 4 do not reach it. T is withdrawn only by a withdraws counted under T's own rule. A quorum's act is undone only by a quorum.
The signer signed T.
The signer is named in T's subject_key_ids, and T's family is not on the kept list below.
The signer is a proxy for a party T names by canonical hash. It holds a live delegates_to chain to that hash whose scope includes consent_revocation. T's family is not on the kept list.
The signer holds a live delegates_to from a party of rules 1 to 3, and the kept list binds it as it binds them.

section.t: Where T names several parties, an admitted withdrawal from one retires T for all of them. A withdrawal reaches forward only: acts under T that the withdrawal has among its ancestors still stand ().

The kept list stops a named party from withdrawing a third party's adverse finding about itself, such as a detection, a licensing decision or a moderation record. lists the families it covers. The named party's route is to contest the row.
A key revocation is never withdrawn. An entity revocation, an occurrence revocation, a key grant, a cosignature already sent and a receipt of acts () are never withdrawn either (CC 2.4.1.1).
Recantation is not covered by these rules. Only T's signer can recant T.

section.name: The End of a Standing
section.t: A standing is what a row confers on a key: a seat, a grant, an owner's binding. A withdrawal or a cut can end it while its holder is still signing. No instant decides which of the holder's acts count. The rows name heads, and a node reads those (CC 2.4.1.1).

dd.t: A row signed in exercise of a standing names the head it is at, in refs.head. The head is the newest its signer holds of the record that seats the standing: the roster version for a seat in a room or a family, and the bundle in force for a grant from a root. A row signed under a root grant names that bundle, and names under the also role stands_on the acceptance of the grant that it stands on. One that names the bundle alone, or names a binding, stands on no acceptance and counts for nobody. Where one row between two keys is the whole record, as an owner's binding is, that row is the head. A row that exercises a standing and names no head concludes nothing, act_names_no_head. An acceptance or a decline names none, since it names the row it answers. A halt names none, since it fires at each node on receipt ().

dl.dt: An end names the head it acts from.

dd.t: A row that ends a standing carries refs.head beside its target. That head is the newest its signer holds. An end with a newer head in its own past concludes nothing, end_names_old_head.

An act with the end in its past does not count under the ended standing. An act at the end's head, at an older head or at a concurrent one counts at its own head, and from the end's head on it is not in force. The end never undoes that count.

Such an act stays in force after the end where a clean receipt of it is held that does not have the end in its past. A receipt is a row of the family act:ack. It names each act it acknowledges under the also role ack, at most 256 of them, and it names no head. It has those acts in its past, and it is clean when that past holds no cut of them by its own key. The receipt is the conferrer's, another holder's of the body the act was done for, or that of a receipter the offer names in receipter. It is never the act's own signer's and never a node's. A receipt changes what is in force, never what counted.

A counted row that ends a standing may state lifts. Then only the count's own receipts keep an act in force. An end by the one whose standing it is lifts nothing, and lifts on such an end is refused, lifts_on_own_end.
An act that another live standing of its signer authorises at its head stands on that standing.

section.t: A device that has not seen the end may sign an act at an older head. That act counts there and is never in force after the end. No reader can tell it from an honest earlier act, and no rule tries.

A key's revocation is read differently, by signed instant: a statement by a revoked key stands where its asserted_at precedes the revocation's revoked_after, and a revocation without that member revokes all (CC 2.4.1.1).

section.name: The Safety Model the Rows Carry
section.t: This section is informative. is normative for every rule it summarises, and the section numbers given are those of .

CEG serves a network with no central operator. No party can enforce a safety rule for the others, so each rule has to be carried by the rows themselves and checked by each node on its own. This section says which member or check carries each property, and what is not claimed.

section.name: Two Planes
section.t: The network has a public plane and a private plane. The CIRIS documents call them the lightnet and the darknet.

The identity plane (lightnet) is public. Key records, announced transport destinations and trust roots are visible to every node, and the plane makes no anonymity claim. A node attributes every inbound message to a key before any handler sees it. A device that has not yet been bound to an owner can still open a connection, but only under its own self-signed key, so it is unowned but never anonymous (CC 3.2).

The group plane (darknet) is derived from the identity plane. Each member of a family or community computes the group's address from directory state it already holds, so the address is never announced. An outsider cannot map an address to a group or fetch its content (CC 5.2, CC 5.4.6). An observer of link traffic can still see which node opens links to some derived address, and the timing and size of that traffic. Members relay for members.

section.name: Consent-Bounded Flow
section.t: The rows apply the idea of contextual integrity: information flows appropriately when the flow matches the norms of the context it came from. Each row signs its own context. iss and author say who sent it, sub and subject_key_ids say whom it is about, and cohort_scope says who may see it. All of these are in the protected header or the payload, so a relay cannot change them without breaking the signature.

A Consumer accepts a row only if it trusts the signer's root or has consented to receive from the signer, and a row reaches no one else (CC 4.4.3.34). A row defaults to the smallest scope that fits its purpose; federation scope, the public commons, is an explicit choice (CC 1.13.3.4). Consent is itself a row, and a subject can withdraw a row about itself (). Content in a private scope is never scanned. Known abuse images are checked for only when content is moved to federation scope or posted to a public room (CC 1.13.3.4).

section.name: Delegation
section.t: Only delegation composes. A Consumer walks the delegates_to graph with a depth cap and a cap on aggregate weight (CC 2.4.1.3, CC 4.1.1). The walk visits each key once, so a cycle adds no reach. A row that closes a cycle is not refused or discounted for it.

section.name: Accountable Key Relationships
section.t: Some parties cannot accept obligations for themselves. The rows give each of them a named human:

list.t: An agent key MUST be bound to a human steward before it is admitted to any community. A node key MUST be so bound before it is admitted to any community other than an infrastructure community (CC 3.2).
A minor has one or more guardians, each bound by a signed row of their own (CC 3.2, CC 3.4.13).

A community names the holders of its moderation duty in its founding record. A seat is two consents, the placer's and the holder's, and it goes only to a member. If no duty holder is left, the community locks to read-only and its members elect one (CC 4.5.4).

section.name: A Bounded Human Halt
section.t: A trust root names a set of human holders. Any one holder can pause the AI agents of the nodes that accepted that root. The halt is one row with one statement, the holder's own, and it fires on receipt with no window. A holder may sign one in advance and keep it sealed (CC 4.2.1.1).

A halt by one holder lapses a fixed time after each node received it: halt_fuse_secs in the charter, 24 hours when absent. It stands longer only if a strict majority of the standing roster confirms it. A strict majority may resume a halt at any time. The confirmation and the resumption are counted rows (): one statement from each holder, over one payload (CC 4.2.1.3).

There is no rate bound on a holder's lone halts. A missed halt is the one failure that cannot be recovered from, so the one-holder stop is never rationed. A rogue holder is answered by the fuse, by a strict majority's resumption, and by removal through a later genesis bundle. Roster changes and recoveries are later bundles, counted over the standing roster (, CC 4.2.6).

A halt pauses the effectful acts of AI agents and does nothing else. It does not stop a node, and it does not touch stored data, messages or network service. An agent checks the latch before every effectful act. A halted agent may still raise a deferral to a human.

The halt is the condition of symmetry between people and the AI agents they make. Consent that cannot be withdrawn was never consent, and withdrawal needs a halt outside the system halted (CC 1.13.2). A root can tell a node to share less, never more. A node that never accepted the root is not affected. Acceptance of a root is a person's row, and a node reads its owner's. An owner leaves a root by withdrawing that one row, for every node and agent the owner holds (CC 3.2); a halt that has already reached a node still binds it (CC 4.2.1).

section.name: What Is Not Claimed
section.t: Where speaks of anonymity, it means anonymity toward outsiders: a group's existence, and what its members do in it, are hidden from non-members. Beyond that:

list.t: The identity plane is not anonymous.

The base design does not resist a global passive observer of traffic. specifies an opt-in Anonymous Tier, using layered onion routing, for deployments that need that protection (CC 1.13.3.1, CC 5.4.6). This document does not describe it.

Members of a group can read, and keep, what the group shares. Ballots within a group are signed rows, accountable to its members. A community may instead hold a secret poll through the census (CC 6.1.9).
Nothing is detected inside private groups. The design declines client-side scanning.

section.t: also states limits that hold against an attacker (CC 2.7.9). Among them:

list.t: A relay can choose the order of delivery, and withhold a row until it is delivered.

A relay can withhold the row that would answer a window until one node's clock has closed it. That node's answer then differs for good from a node that held the row in time. The halt's fuse is one such window; a fresh halt is the remedy.
Whoever holds an ended key's private half can revive it. Only the key's own revocation makes its end final.
Keys that met a past count can fork on a past head. Whoever controls a new reader's first view can make a wrong head stick.

section.t: On aggregation, correlated sources are discounted, and fully correlated sources count as one. Sources that stay independent on every measured act and coordinate only on one decisive act show no correlation until that act. No measure over the past can see them (CC 6.1.2.3).

section.name: Relationship to SCITT
section.t: This section is informative.

section.name: Roles

texttable.title: SCITT roles and their CEG counterparts
texttable.c: Issuer
The signer, named by iss.
Signed Statement
A statement: one COSE_Sign1 by one signer.
Registration Policy
The admission checks of .
Transparency Service
A service a root's charter or a room's record names for its heads, or one a host trusts by its owner's acceptance edge; CEG fixes none (, , ).
Receipt
A COSE Receipt from a service's own log: for a registered head, or the receipt a host requires before it runs admitted code (, ).
Transparent Statement
A statement with a receipt in its unprotected header.
Relying Party
A Consumer.

section.t: A CEG statement is a COSE_Sign1 with iss and sub in the CWT Claims header of , as requires. It can be presented to a SCITT Transparency Service as it stands. A counted row is several Signed Statements over one payload. A Transparency Service would register each one separately; CEG relates them by the row id ().

dd.t: The composite signature uses the private-use COSE algorithm identifier -70100. A Transparency Service or Relying Party must support that construction to verify a statement. Its parent drafts and are not yet published as RFCs. The header labels -70001, -70002 and -70003 are also from the private-use range.
The content type application/vnd.ciris.row+cbor and the typ values ceg-row/2 and the three object kinds are used without registration. This document requests no IANA action for them.

CEG fixes no Transparency Service and no registrar. A node admits a row by its own checks, and what it serves is decided by trust the reader chose. Registration is asked for in three places. A root's charter may name the services its lineage heads are registered with, a room's record may name them for its accountable streams (), and a host runs code a row admits only once it holds a receipt from a service its owner trusts (). Each service is SCITT's own and keeps its own log. Its receipt shows registration and confers no standing.

has the Transparency Service evaluate its policy and requires the policy itself to be registered, so that Auditors can reproduce the decision. The CEG checks read the payload as well as the headers. They are fixed by rather than registered as statements. Any party can reproduce an admission decision from the row and the checks, but the checks are not themselves on a log.

A SCITT Receipt is issued at registration by the service, and a CEG receipt is the same: each service issues its own, from its own log. Nothing requires a receipt when a row is admitted. Attaching to a root that names services requires a receipt quorum for its head, an accountable stream head is published by one, and running the code a row admits requires a receipt from a service the host trusts (, ). A holder may add a receipt to a statement's unprotected header.

leaves to a Relying Party how many Receipts it asks for. fixes a count: a head is receipted at a strict majority of the services named for it, and only services independent of the lineage count (). A lineage whose charter names no services has no such check. Its holders can show different heads to different peers until a row crosses between them.

SCITT leaves the meaning of a statement to its issuer. CEG fixes the five row types and requires every claim to name a registered family, so a Consumer can interpret any admitted row without out-of-band agreement.
A CEG verifier can answer Waiting on a key or a row it does not hold, and hold the statement inert (). A SCITT Registration Policy admits or refuses.

defines no identifier for a Signed Statement. The CEG statement id is a name of this profile (). It covers the protected header and the payload, as the COSE Sig_structure does with an empty external_aad, and is a different digest from one over the Sig_structure or over the whole COSE_Sign1.

section.name: Registering a Head
section.t: Revision -03 of this document proposed that the signer of a log's head register each head with a Transparency Service as a Signed Statement. states that rule, and describes it. A stream's head is a stream:head row, a lineage's head is the bundle in force, and each is a Signed Statement a service registers as it stands. The services are named in signed bytes: by a root's charter for its lineage, and by a room's record for its accountable streams.

Two registered heads at one position are proof of equivocation, signed by the equivocating keys and held by a third party. A head that is registered with no service is single-signer, and its readers compare heads themselves.
This is the method of Section 8 of , where a chain head is carried to a Transparency Service as a signed statement that also carries the derived root.

section.name: Lifecycle of an Agent Decision
section.t: This section is informative.

Other individual drafts record AI agent actions as a sequence of logged events: an authorisation before the act, a record of the act, and a refusal where the agent declined. The Artificial Intelligence Governance Architecture logs agent activity in Merkle trees and is the closest in aim. PALA-1 defines a tamper-evident audit record for inference runtimes and carries its chain head to a Transparency Service. In CEG the same events are rows. The reasoning steps before an act are rows in the decision families of . The act is recorded by one row whose dimension is trace:complete:v1, ending in a terminal result. That trace, its components, levels and signing are specified in , and the context manifest of each model call within it in ; this document specifies only the row that carries it. A completed action, a refusal, and a deferral to a human are the same kind of row with different terminal results, so a Consumer reads all three the same way. Authority to act, and any transfer of it, is a delegates_to row.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This section follows the guidance of .

dd.t: A verifier that re-encodes a decoded payload before checking the signature can accept bytes the signer never signed, or reject bytes it did. A verifier MUST check the bytes received and refuse any encoding that is not deterministic. Implementations should test against the refusals of non-deterministic encodings in .

The protected header and the payload are signed; the unprotected header is not. No admission check reads the unprotected header; the host's receipt check reads it and grants nothing. Who a row is about and who may see it are in the signed bytes, so a relay cannot redirect a validly signed row.

Both halves sign one representative that names the composite label, so neither half verifies alone. A forger must break both ML-DSA-65 and Ed25519. A verifier MUST NOT accept a statement on one half. A key is one composite key, and a statement whose signer's key record is not held is Waiting, never Valid.
kid and iss carry full 32-byte thumbprints, not short fingerprints. A verifier resolves kid to a key record and verifies with the full composite key that record holds.

iss is signed by whoever signs the statement, so a signature that verifies does not show that the signer is the identity iss names. A verifier MUST check that kid's key is a key of iss () before it treats the statement as that issuer's. A Relying Party that reads iss from a statement it has not verified through step 8 of reads an unchecked claim.

dl.dt: A name is not a signature.

dd.t: A row id, a statement id and an object id are digests of bytes. Two parties that hold the same id hold the same bytes, and nothing more follows. An id is computed without any key, so anyone can compute the id of a statement nobody signed. A statement id leaves out the signature and the unprotected header, so a statement with a corrupted signature has the id of the valid one. An id is evidence of a statement only together with a verification of that statement (, ).

A rotation record links a new key to an identity only with the old key's statement and the new key's own. A verifier MUST NOT accept a new key on the new key's word, or on the old key's alone. Two successors of one key hand on nothing, so a thief of an old key who rotates it cannot displace the holder's own rotation: both are refused until one rotation names both. The thief can block the hand-on in that way. leaves the pair to the key's owner, who binds one successor (CC 2.4.1.1, ).
The withdrawal rules let parties other than the signer retract a row. The rules in stop a subject from removing adverse findings about itself, and stop any single key from undoing a quorum's act.

A head that is registered with no Transparency Service stands on its signers alone. They can show different histories to different peers until the heads are compared. A root whose charter names no services, and a best-effort stream, are in this case ().

A window closed on one node's clock, such as the halt's fuse, is read differently by nodes that held a row at different instants. states which readings depend on a node's clock and gives them no meaning beyond that node's own (CC 2.7.9).

The 1 MiB limit applies to the deterministic encoding. An implementation that reads an unbounded input in order to find out whether it fits is open to memory exhaustion. Each write path needs its own read limit.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: This section follows the guidance of .

dd.t: iss names a signer's genesis key and does not change when the signing key rotates. Every row a signer makes can therefore be linked to every other. Statements carry thumbprints, not human-chosen labels.
A canonical identifier is a hash of a platform, entity kind and identifier. Where the identifier space is small, the hash can be reversed by enumeration.
A row whose content is guessable, such as a ballot, carries a random salt in its payload. Without it, the row id would confirm a guess.
cohort_scope limits which nodes may receive a row. It is signed, so a relay cannot widen it. It does not encrypt the row; a node inside the audience can read and keep it.

A withdraws row stops a claim from standing. It does not remove the original row from nodes that already hold it. Members minted blind () can be erased by dropping their disclosures, which alters no signed byte. defines a separate removal procedure for the rest.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)

abstract.t: The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size, and extensibility without the need for version negotiation. These design goals make it different from earlier binary serializations such as ASN.1 and MessagePack.

This document obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial improvements, new details, and errata fixes while keeping full compatibility with the interchange format of RFC 7049. It does not create a new version of the format.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

front.title: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL): A Notational Convention to Express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and JSON Data Structures

abstract.t: This document proposes a notational convention to express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures (RFC 7049). Its main goal is to provide an easy and unambiguous way to express structures for protocol messages and data formats that use CBOR or JSON.

front.title: Additional Control Operators for the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL)

abstract.t: The Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL), standardized in RFC 8610, provides "control operators" as its main language extension point.

The present document defines a number of control operators that were not yet ready at the time RFC 8610 was completed:.plus,.cat, and.det for the construction of constants;.abnf/.abnfb for including ABNF (RFC 5234 and RFC 7405) in CDDL specifications; and.feature for indicating the use of a non-basic feature in an instance.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) "typ" (type) Header Parameter

abstract.t: This specification adds the equivalent of the JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) "typ" (type) header parameter to CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE). This enables the benefits of explicit typing (as defined in RFC 8725, "JSON Web Token Best Current Practices") to be brought to COSE objects. The syntax of the COSE type header parameter value is the same as the existing COSE content type header parameter.

front.title: CBOR Web Token (CWT) Claims in COSE Headers

abstract.t: This document describes how to include CBOR Web Token (CWT) claims in the header parameters of any CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) structure. This functionality helps to facilitate applications that wish to make use of CWT claims in encrypted COSE structures and/or COSE structures featuring detached signatures, while having some of those claims be available before decryption and/or without inspecting the detached payload. Another use case is using CWT claims with payloads that are not CWT Claims Sets, including payloads that are not CBOR at all.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Key Thumbprint

abstract.t: This specification defines a method for computing a hash value over a CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Key. It specifies which fields within the COSE Key structure are included in the cryptographic hash computation, the process for creating a canonical representation of these fields, and how to hash the resulting byte sequence. The resulting hash value, referred to as a "thumbprint", can be used to identify or select the corresponding key.

front.title: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings

abstract.t: This document describes the commonly used base 64, base 32, and base 16 encoding schemes. It also discusses the use of line-feeds in encoded data, use of padding in encoded data, use of non-alphabet characters in encoded data, use of different encoding alphabets, and canonical encodings. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)

abstract.t: This document describes elliptic curve signature scheme Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA). The algorithm is instantiated with recommended parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves. An example implementation and test vectors are provided.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While Verifiable Data Structures (VDSs) have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility and interoperability between different transparency services as well as compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.

front.title: CBOR Common Deterministic Encoding (CDE)

abstract.t:
CBOR (STD 94, RFC 8949) defines the concept of "Deterministically Encoded CBOR" in its Section 4.2, determining one specific way to encode each particular CBOR value. This definition is instantiated by "core requirements", providing some flexibility for application specific decisions; this makes it harder than necessary to offer Deterministic Encoding as a selectable feature of generic CBOR encoders.
The present specification documents the Best Current Practice for CBOR _Common Deterministic Encoding_ (CDE), which can be shared by a large set of applications with potentially diverging detailed application requirements.
The document also discusses the desire for partial implementations, which can be another reason for constraining CBOR encoders, and singles out the encoding constraint "definite-length-only" as a likely constraint to be used in application protocol and media type definitions.
This specification updates RFC 8949 in that it provides clarifications and definitions of additional terms as well as more examples and explanatory text; it does not make technical changes to RFC 8949.
